1:
The figure is read the same way by all of them. Gill says the wind is no more beneficial than air to a man who opens his mouth and fills himself with it: it stands for labour in vain, a man getting nothing by all his pains, the same as sowing the wind and reaping the whirlwind. Calvin puts it more bodily: when one gulps the wind he seems to fill his mouth, his throat and his whole stomach, and there is nothing but air, no nourishment. Henry adds the persistence: he feeds on vain hopes of assistance from man while he is at variance with God, and when disappointed still pursues the same game, panting after what he cannot catch hold of, and which would not nourish him if he could.

The east wind sharpens the charge from empty to deadly. Clarke says the counsels are not only empty but destructive, the east wind being everywhere a parching, wasting, injurious wind. Calvin says other winds bring rain or some other advantage, while this brings nothing but drought and storms. Ellicott quotes a traveller on it: the wind is more frequent in winter and early spring, and if it continues long the tender vegetation is parched up and a year of famine follows, man and beast feeling sickly while it prevails; hence what is unpleasant and revolting in life is compared to the east wind, destructiveness and emptiness combining in it.

The lies are the treaties. Henry reads them as multiplied leagues with the neighbours, all of which will prove deceitful, and warns that those who stay themselves upon lies will still covet to increase them, as if many lies twisted together would make one truth, or many broken reeds one sound support. The Assyrians were to be secured by a solemn league, though that potent prince will be a slave to his word no longer than he pleases, and the Egyptians by a present, though having got the bribe they dropped the cause. Clarke says it shortly, that Egypt abandoned him and Assyria oppressed him; Wesley notes that the oil was not common oil for trade but rich and precious oils, sent to procure friendship. Calvin turns falsehood inward, to the impostures by which the people deceived themselves, sharpening their wits to deceive God and so involving themselves in fatal snares; and he takes desolation as the cause of desolation: you shall at last perceive that you have gained nothing by your counsels but destruction.

The turn to Judah surprises Calvin, who had earlier called that tribe faithful with the saints. His answer is that the praise was comparative and belonged to the worship which as yet prevailed at Jerusalem, not to their manners, and that the ten tribes were the less excusable because the temple stood in their sight. He touches Judah only in passing, being a teacher set over Israel, and names that kingdom to strike terror: if God will not spare the Jews, the others cannot hope to escape. Gill fills in the history: Judah and Benjamin were faithful in the first times of the apostasy of Israel and afterwards degenerated into idolatry, particularly in the time of Ahaz. Henry draws the rule: being right in the main things will not exempt men from correction, and therefore should not exempt them from reproof for the things wherein they are wrong.

Whose name Jacob is here is not settled. Ellicott says it refers to the northern kingdom; Wesley takes it of both, since Ephraim and Judah are alike of Jacob and both have corrupted themselves; Keil and Delitzsch make the name the link to the patriarch himself, whom the Israelites as his descendants were to imitate, and set the whole division under the charge that Israel has not kept the ways of its father but has fallen into the practice of Canaan.
3:
The grasp in the womb is read as election, not as courage. Gill takes it as a presage and pledge that Jacob should get the birthright and blessing, and says the patriarch is named here to show how far his posterity had degenerated: the father a hero from the womb and the sons transgressors from it. Calvin will not let it be an act at all: Jacob did not by choice or design lay hold on the heel, for he was then enclosed in the womb and could do nothing by his own power; it was God who guided the hand of the infant, and by that sign testified his adoption to be gratuitous. He presses it against pride of descent: they had no merit of their own to show for their difference from Esau and his posterity; God of his own good pleasure chose them, and the ingratitude is the baser because he had put them under obligation before they were born. Wesley says the strength was not of nature but of grace, well employed betimes.

How a man prevails over God is Calvin’s next difficulty, and his answer is a distribution of power. Jacob prevailed not of himself, but God had so ordered his own strength that the greater part of it was in Jacob. Speaking of the daily contests with which God exercises the godly, Calvin says that God fights with us with his left hand and defends us with his right, assailing us weakly while stretching out his right hand to defend, so that we come out of the struggle victorious. Harsh as it sounds, it sets forth the goodness of God, who is more glorified in defending us than in overwhelming us, which he could do with one breath of his mouth.

The weeping is assigned two ways. Calvin knows an explanation that gives it to the angel, as one who owns himself unequal and throws himself on the ground, so that the request to be let go was a confession of defeat; but he prefers the patriarch, since weeping may be taken for the humility the faithful bring to God, and it became him well, for he did not depart whole. His thigh was dislocated and he was lame all his life, and yet, worn out with weariness, he did not wish the angel gone but held him as by force: I would rather contend with thee and be wholly consumed than let thee go before thou bless me.

Who the angel was is settled the same way by two of them. Gill sets aside a string of proposals, that it was a created angel, or the archangel some name, or a guardian angel such as many suppose, or an evil angel set against Jacob, of whom he would never have sought a blessing; it was the uncreated Angel, the Son of God, called an Angel by office, not by nature. Wesley agrees: no created angel but the Messiah, eternal God by nature and essence, angel by office and voluntary undertaking. Clarke says only that the Angel represented the invisible God, and that the weeping is not in the earlier history.

Where God was found closes it. Clarke says it was at Bethel that God made those glorious promises to Jacob about his posterity. Calvin takes it of the first meeting, when Jacob fled through fear of his brother and thought himself cast away and destitute of all aid: God presented himself when the holy man hoped no such thing, and Jacob prevailed later because God had long before begun to embrace him in his love. On the closing words Calvin refuses the emendation that would make God speak with him rather than with us, adopted only because interpreters find no sense in the phrase as it stands, and refuses as strained the reading that makes the us prophets of a later day.
5:
The name is given to fix who the wrestler was. Gill says the God Jacob had power over, the Angel he prevailed with at Bethel, is he whose name is Jehovah, Lord of hosts in heaven and in earth, of all the angels and of the church militant, the Captain of their salvation; the title is set down to show the greatness of the person Jacob wrestled with and the grace by which he condescended to be overpowered. Wesley says the same of the constancy: he that appeared and spake and promised the blessing was the eternal and unchangeable God, who can perform his promise and execute his threat, a most terrible enemy and a most desirable friend.

Ellicott alone asks what the hosts are. He judges them probably the stars, conceived of as celestial spirits standing above the throne of God on the right hand and on the left, to be identified with the sons of God who are described as presenting themselves in council and elsewhere as his ministers. The memorial he takes for the name, and the name for the self-existent One who nevertheless came into personal relations with Israel.

The exhortation that follows is drawn straight from the unchangeableness. Clarke bids them turn because he is the same and cannot change: seek him as faithfully and as fervently as Jacob did, and you will find him the same merciful and compassionate Being. Gill addresses it to Judah, with whom the Lord had the controversy, and urges it from their descent from so great a man; turning supposes a going astray, and means turning from idols and from all vain confidences by renewed acts of faith and repentance, which cannot be performed aright without grace and strength from God. Ellicott corrects the connective: rather than therefore, he would read, But do thou return to thy God, and finds in it an implied contrast between the patriarch and his degenerate descendants.

Calvin uses the command to close off the excuses. They did worship gods and wearied themselves in their superstitions, and he cuts the handle from that subterfuge by bidding them turn to their God: let them confess they are apostates who have rejected the law delivered to them by the true God. He notes that God is here called the God of Israel not to honour them but to reproach them, since they had willingly and designedly cast off the worship of the one who had made himself known to them.

What surprises Calvin is the order. The prophet begins with the second table, mercy and judgment, and only afterwards adds piety towards God, in two words that include the whole teaching of that table. Calvin grants the order is neither natural nor legitimate, but says the prophets do not observe order strictly, and that this one had the best reason for it: repentance is better tested by the second table than by divine worship, since hypocrites dissemble and hide themselves with wonderful coverings, so that the Lord applies a touchstone, drawing them into the light and exposing their frauds, robberies, cruelty, perjuries and thefts. Let it be made evident whether the repentance is feigned or sincere; if a man acts justly and uprightly towards his neighbours, that is sure evidence.

The waiting is made to carry the rest. By the word hope, Calvin says, the prophet requires faith first, then the prayer which arises from it, and the thanksgiving which necessarily follows, so that the whole worship of God is briefly included, a part standing for the whole, in that one word. Wesley spells the duties out instead: show kindness to all who need it; wrong none, but with justice in dealings, in judicatures and in public offices render every one their due; and in public worship and private duties serve God alone, letting idols have neither sacrifice, prayer, praise, nor trust.
7:
The first word of the verse is a name, not a trade. Gill notes that being a merchant is nothing worthy of dispraise in itself, but that this one was a fraudulent dealer, more like a descendant of Canaan by his manners than of Jacob; the Canaanites dealing much in merchandise, their name became a common word for a merchant, as a Chaldean did for an astrologer. Ellicott holds that the force of the words is obscured in the English, and would translate, As for Canaan, in his hand are false balances, he loves cheating. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a substitution: Israel is not a Jacob who wrestles with God but has become Canaan, seeking its advantage in deceit and wrong; and they set aside a reading that makes the fraud religious, an offering of false show for true reverence, since the prophet speaks of weights and of violence. Calvin reads the name as a word thrown in indignation at men who held up their descent as a shield and called themselves a holy people: you are not the children of Abraham, you falsely boast of a name that cannot suit you, for you are Canaan.

The cheating itself is described in trade terms. Clarke says he kept, as many in all ages have, a weight and a weight, a heavy one to buy with and a light one to sell by. Henry watches the performance: he delivers his goods by weight and measure as though he would be very exact, and under colour of doing right does the greatest wrong; God has his eye on merchants when they are weighing their goods, and though trades are made mysteries by the wit of man, it is a pity they become mysteries of iniquity by his sin. He presses the last clause hardest: to oppress is bad enough, but to love it is worse, for such a man sins for the sake of sinning and takes pleasure in overreaching those who do not suspect him. Wesley sums it in a line: Ephraim is so far from being as Jacob that you may account him a Canaanite.

The defence he makes is prosperity. Gill says they got abundance of riches and concluded that their manner of dealing was not criminal, or at least not so bad as the prophets represented, and so promised themselves impunity. Henry notes that he neither denies the charge nor confesses it, but insists on his justification: whatever you make of it, I have made a good hand of it. Calvin marks the adversative force of the opening particle: they laughed at reproof because prosperity looked like a token of favour, and nothing is more to be feared than having our eyes dazzled by a desirable state of things.

The second boast goes further, and Calvin calls it worse. To despise God because he deals kindly is not to be endured, but to conclude that he would not have favoured us had we not been exempt from every fault is a diabolical madness. Wesley says he hugs himself on the close carriage of his affairs, so that no great crime can be found in him, none that is sin, that is, any great enormity. Ellicott renders it, all my earnings bring me not guilt as would be sin, that is, guilt requiring expiation. Clarke turns on the trade itself: none are so full of professions of equity as those who are all the while endeavouring to overreach, and he says he has heard such language over and over when he knew every word of it false.

The answer is put briefly. Keil and Delitzsch say the Lord meets the delusion that they had become great by their own exertion by reminding them that he has been the God of Israel from the land of Egypt hither, and that they owe him all their prosperity.
9:
The opening clause is a reminder with a purpose. Calvin says God reproaches them for having forgotten their redemption, the memory of which ought ever to have flourished among them, and that by naming himself their God from the land of Egypt he points out the end for which he redeemed them: I delivered thee that thou mightest be for ever bound to me, and when I freed that people from a cruel tyranny I at the same time acquired an eternal kingdom. They were like the dead when he stretched out his hand to them; they owed him themselves and all theirs, since he purchased them for a peculiar possession, and it is an ingratitude not to be endured that they should petulantly reject the prophets who speak in his name.

What follows is either the kindest or the harshest thing in the chapter, and the voices divide. Gill takes it wholly as promise, spoken to Judah after the call to repentance and to be fulfilled in the times of the Messiah, especially the latter part of them, when all Israel shall return and be saved, redeemed from a worse than Egyptian bondage, from the bondage of sin, Satan, the law, the world and death. Clarke reads the same words as a threatening: I will reduce you to as miserable a state in captivity as you often were through your transgressions in the wilderness; and he adds plainly that he does not think the feast of tabernacles is referred to at all. Wesley keeps the feast and the blessing together, taking the tents for all the comforts given them, expressed proverbially in allusion to the joy they had at that feast.

Ellicott holds the two senses at once, the neatest solution offered. He takes the verse for a moral restoration set out as a return to the old ideal of a simple agricultural life, in which every good gift is received directly from the hand of God. To the true theocratic spirit that condition is one of real blessedness; but to the worldly and grasping Canaan of the earlier verses it would come as a threat of expulsion, desolation and despair.

Calvin canvasses three readings before giving his own. Some take the tabernacles loosely for houses and find a promise that God would not cease to show mercy however unworthy they were, by an ancient agreement giving the land to the posterity of Abraham for their perpetual rest; that exposition Calvin thinks unsuitable. Others make it a reproof for neglecting the yearly festival appointed to keep the redemption in memory, so that God complains he has effected nothing by the rite, being now rejected and his prophets without authority; that sense Calvin calls frigid. Others again take it as the threat, that God will drive them out to dwell in tents as they did in the desert; this he does not reject, but he thinks the words carry something more emphatic.

His own reading is that a second redemption is announced. God says indirectly that there is need of a new deliverance to bind the people more closely to himself: I see you are unmindful of my former redemption and esteem it as nothing, as though obsolete, and I must lose all my labour unless the memory of my ancient favour be renewed. It is necessary to eject thee again from thy heritage and to restore thee again, and that in a manner unusual and least expected, that thou mayest understand that I am thy Redeemer. As your first redemption avails nothing, he has God say, I will add a second, that you may at length repent and know how much you are indebted to me. The closing phrase Calvin refuses to read of any perpetual compact, taking it of the manner of proceeding in the desert, when the people came together for sacrifice out of their camps.
10:
The verse inventories the means God had used. Clarke turns it into a list: I have used every means and employed every method to instruct and save you; I have sent prophets, who spake plainly, exhorting and beseeching you to return; they have had divine visions which they declared and interpreted; they have used similitudes, symbols, metaphors and allegories to fix your attention; and alas, all is in vain.

Calvin takes the same list as the removal of an excuse. Men evade the judgment of God as long as they can plead ignorance, and the prophet denies that this people fell for want of information: they had been warned by prophets sent in succession, and were become as it were wilfully rebellious. The words may be read that God spoke upon his prophets, depositing with them the doctrine which ought to have restored the people; and not by one method only, for he accumulated visions and endeavoured every way possible to bring them to a sound mind. Calvin adds that God speaks here after the manner of men, since he might if he chose effect it by the secret movement of his Spirit; and he turns the reproach on his own readers, who see how the world hardens itself against warning and how long the Lord bears with those who scoff. Gill takes the speaking otherwise, referring it not to the prophets of old but to the apostles and teachers of the gospel, whose word is the voice of Christ speaking in them.

The question that follows has a laugh in it. Calvin calls it ironical: the prophet scorns men who delighted in vices so gross and are as yet doubtful, forsooth, whether they bear any blame; whatever pretences they seek, their glosses contain nothing solid but are disguises which avail nothing before God. Gill offers a string of senses: is there idolatry in Gilead, strange in a city of the priests and of refuge, or is there none, as the priests pretend who say they worship the true God in their images, or is there iniquity there only? Other places, he answers, are as guilty and must expect the same fate.

Whether the ruin is behind or ahead divides them. Clarke says the town beyond Jordan had already been brought under subjection by the Assyrian, and the one on this side shall share the same fate, being now as idolatrous. Ellicott makes both past, translating, If Gilead be worthless, surely they have become nought, and referring it to a desolating invasion attested in the conqueror’s own mutilated inscriptions, where a city is said to have been joined in its whole extent to Assyria. He infers that Gilgal too felt that heavy hand, or that its people fled and the shrines became deserted ruins, for from that time forth we hear no more of Gilgal as a religious centre. He notes that others take the words as prophecy of a calamity still to come, and that the word for heaps plays on the name of the place.

What the heaps are is agreed. Calvin objects to a rendering of Jerome that makes them sacrifice to oxen and finds the calves reprehended here, and to his placing Gilgal in Judah, which was then free from these defilements. The comparison Calvin explains from the field: as a man gathers the stones of a stony field into heaps that he may drive his plough more easily, so every one raises an altar for himself, a hillock in his own ground. It had looked a diligence worthy of praise to multiply altars and spare neither expense nor labour; but God will be worshipped alone, and will have piety attested by obedience to his word alone. Wesley says only that the altars were for number like stones gathered out of plowed land, and Clarke that they occur everywhere, the whole land being given to idolatry.
12:
The retrospect returns to the patriarch, and Gill fixes the place. The field of Syria is Padanaram, since Padan means a field and Aram is Syria; and the flight is the one made for fear of Esau, though Gill reports interpreters who take it of the later flight from Laban into Gilead, which would make the verse an aggravation of the sin of that place, whose people defiled with idolatry the ground that had sheltered their ancestor. The words, Gill says, will not bear it. Ellicott takes the verse as resuming the retrospect over patriarchal history, and draws the comfort from it: notwithstanding the loneliness and humble position of the patriarch, God took care of him, and he won the mighty name of Israel and gave it to his descendants.

Clarke counts the years: seven served for the younger daughter and seven more keeping sheep for the elder, the patriarch having been cheated by his uncle, who gave him the wrong wife first and then made him serve again before confirming the first engagement. Clarke also answers the objection that the fact stands here isolated: in a detached sentence the prophet speaks of the low estate of their ancestor, and how amply the providence of God provided for him, and that is all the connection the place requires.

Calvin makes the same low estate a rebuke. The prophet employs another kind of reproof, that they never considered from what source they had proceeded; he touches it designedly, since the people boasted so boldly of their eminence, imagining themselves nobler than the common sort. Jacob your father, he has God ask, who was he? What was his condition, his nobility, his power, his dignity according to the flesh? He was a fugitive from his own country, and his father before him only a sojourner; in Syria he lived with his uncle but was treated no better than a worthless slave, and kept sheep. Go now and boast of your dignity.

The coming out of Egypt Calvin calls a second nativity. He knows a reading that sets the two in contrast, as though it ran, though you were born of a poor and ignoble man, God gave you Moses to be the minister of your liberation; but he prefers the simpler course, that the prophet shows first their origin from Jacob and then their second origin, when God begat them again in bringing them out of Egypt. They were very miserable there, and did not come out by their own valour; one man alone extended his hand to them, and he had been sent for that end.

Who the two prophets are is not answered alike. Gill and Wesley both name Moses, Gill calling him the prophet who by way of eminency is so called, and a type of Christ, the Redeemer of his people from sin, Satan, the world, the law and death; Wesley adds that the preserving was in the wilderness, and that the aim of the passage is to prevent their vain boasting of their ancestors. Clarke divides them: by a prophet, Moses, the Lord brought them out, and by a prophet, Joshua, was he preserved, for Joshua brought them into the promised land, and when they passed the Jordan at Gilgal he received the covenant of circumcision, and yet this same place was now made the seat of idolatry. How blind and how ungrateful, he says. Ellicott keeps to Moses and hears a hint that the Lord would yet again save Israel from a worse than Egyptian bondage by the words and warnings of a prophet.

Calvin sums it as a speech: I chose your father, and not for any dignity in the world; I afterwards redeemed you out of Egypt, and in that coming forth there was nothing that you did. How great then is your ingratitude, that you do not own me as your Redeemer.
14:
Ellicott hears the tone change at the name. The rift in the clouds closes again and another severe rebuke follows, and Jacob and Israel give place to the proud tribal name of Ephraim; it is this portion of the whole house of Israel that incurs the charge. He would read, Ephraim hath provoked bitter feeling, and takes the bloodguiltiness of Moloch sacrifices and other iniquity for what God will not remove.

What the bitterness is divides the two who look hardest at the word. Gill takes it of the manner and of the matter together: it was God whom the ten tribes provoked, notwithstanding all the favours they and their ancestors had received from him, and they provoked him to bitter anger and vehement wrath; or the word may be read with bitternesses, that is, with their sins, which are in their own nature bitter and displeasing to God and in their effects bring bitterness and death upon those who commit them, meaning particularly their idolatry and all that belonged to it, their idols, high places and altars. Calvin will not take the word adverbially at all. He knows that some render it bitternesses, so that Israel provoked God to bitterness; but since the word is elsewhere used of high places, and since the prophet is inveighing avowedly against Israel and their vicious worship, Calvin does not doubt that it points to the high places in which they appointed their false and impious modes of worship, so that Ephraim, having in so many ways immersed themselves in superstitions, provoked God in them.

The clause about blood turns on a word that faces two ways. Calvin observes that the verb signifies both to pour out and to remain, so that some render it, his blood shall remain, and others, shall be poured upon him; but he says this makes little difference to the sense, since the prophet intends to show that Ephraim must suffer the punishment of their impiety and shall not at last escape from the hand of God, but shall receive the wages of their iniquities. Wesley takes the blood as their own doing twice over: he shall bear the punishment of all his blood, both his murders of the innocent and his own guilt. Clarke takes it of guilt not removed, and matches it with the saying that the wrath of God abides on the man who will not believe, since he rejects the only way in which he can be saved; because they said they saw, their sin remained, standing charged against them. Their miseries and destruction, he adds, are of their own procuring, and their perdition is of themselves, for God is as merciful as he is just.

The last words name the offended party, and both Calvin and Wesley find the title pointed. Wesley reads the reproach as what Ephraim had cast upon the prophets, upon the worshippers of God, and upon God himself, in preferring idols before him; and his Lord is God, who is Lord of all. Calvin marks that God is called the Lord of Israel though Israel had shaken off the yoke and alienated themselves from his service. They cannot escape his authority though they have spurned his law; though they have grown wanton in their superstitions, they shall yet know that they remain under his hand and power, and that they effect nothing by this their petulance, for the Lord will not lose the right which he obtained for himself by redeeming Israel.
